html:
Last year, I sold my parents’ co-op apartment in Queens, after holding on to it for two decades and paying the monthly maintenance fees – even though I lived 2,500 miles away in Los Angeles. I grew up there; those three-and-a-half rooms, overstuffed with modest furniture and childhood souvenirs, were imprinted on my skin. During infrequent trips east, sitting on one of the cozy cream couches in the living room of my inherited New York sanctuary – with its 40-year-old cupboards and old-fashioned bathroom mirror – I could almost feel my parents’ presence.

I never got to say goodbye, but if I close my eyes tight, I can still see my beautiful train wrecks – aka, my parents – on vacation with me in Playa del Carmen, south of Cancún, on 10 December 2004. They are sitting in the back of our rental car, dusty but cheerful, on the way to the Tulum ruins. My so-not-thin father, Karl, is hungry, for a change. My mother, Violet, is impatient from the suffocating Mexican heat. So rather than listen to them argue, I pull over to the side of the road. It is scorchingly dry. My mind, too, is parched and dull from their nonstop pestering. But I am used to it: arguing is their love language.

The locals tell me el restaurante is across the road, so I start the car back up, go to the worn Stop sign, then move behind a large truck, thinking the driver is about to make what they call a retorno, or U-turn.

But the truck doesn’t move. Why is it just sitting in the middle of the road? We are in the middle of the road and he’s not turning. My brain is in slow motion when I notice a taxi speeding toward us, so close, so fast.

I went to one hospital, and Ma and Pa to others

Why am I crushed between the seatbelt and the car door? Why is my ma unconscious? Her owl-like glasses crushed against her sweet, soft face, which had amazingly few wrinkles for a woman in her 70s. Why is my father screaming: ‘Violet, wake up!’

I reach the hospital and am put in a wheelchair. Those who speak English tell me Mexico is a poor country, ambulances need the business, so the drivers were fighting with each other over who to take where – and that’s why I went to one hospital, and Ma and Pa to others.

My hospital bed is near the taxi guy who hit our car. The doctors tell me the driver will be OK, just shards of glass in his face. He cries, knowing I am near him.

‘Please help me stand up so I can find my parents,’ I say. But the rude nurse tells me: ‘You could go to jail if you don’t cooperate’ and ‘Sit still, we need to monitor you.’ Then the US Consulate calls. My ma is dead.

The nurses feed me papaya slices because, in my basic high-school Spanish, I asked for fruit and they thought I wanted only that for every meal. I notice irony, like the fact that my parents loved fried foods and I would lecture them about eating healthy. Yet now Ma is dead; she could have eaten anything she wanted. And there was a beautiful serendipity with my orthopaedic doctor, who holds my hand and tells me, in broken English, that he was on call at my mother’s hospital. He tried everything to help her, but for her frail, petite body, a massive haemorrhage was too much. At least she did not die alone.

Initially, the police are puzzled: why was my car in the middle of the road, and did I even know my passengers? When the policewoman and detective visit my hospital room, I tearfully explain. My passengers were my parents. With their round bellies after retirement, they had protested wearing seatbelts, so I put them in the back.

As I tell them about the retorno lane, where the truck blocked our way forward, leaving us in the path of the speeding taxi, the policewoman starts crying. She knows the area and knew the truck had been abandoned. I was at the wrong place, wrong time.

Back home, the tumour is taken out, but he’s a vegetable

So… good news, I am no longer blamed for the accident or facing Cancún jail. The US Consulate helps free me from the Mexican police, who return my mother’s rings. And I’ve no broken bones, just contusions; give it a few months and I’ll be able to walk with a cane.

Worse news, my father is acting strangely. They’ve found a large non-cancerous brain tumour, growing in his head for 20 years and no one knew. Yet it made sense. He is more forgetful, no longer enjoying the use of forks and knives. One afternoon, in Queens, he’d brought down my luggage and stood holding my computer in the pouring rain, no umbrella, until the taxi came.

I beg his insurance to medevac us to New York City, and they do. The triumph is short lived. Back home, the tumour is taken out, but he’s a vegetable. They move him to a nursing home, and he’s too sick even for a place like that. Three months later, he’s dead, too.

That moment when I touched his cheek in the funeral home will always stay with me. Refrigerated, his skin was cold. You look good, Daddy, I half-smiled inside to myself. My ma, on the other hand, had to be embalmed to fly back to New York. She looked jarringly unreal, like a doll.

But our old apartment was the coziest, safest place in the world. In recent years, my cousin lectured me about the financial cost: ‘You do know they are never coming back, right?’

I was distracted by the frayed photobooks Ma kept crammed in the fake-wood bookcases. I found myself lingering, squeezing long-forgotten memories back into my brain. Checking the pockets of my father’s large winter coats, I found one of the many square handkerchiefs my ma would stuff into them. Still neatly folded, yellowed in spots from old snot, it was a joy to clutch in my hands.

Seeing the photos documenting my life, I was grateful to my ma, who commanded my father and me to take hundreds of them. In one of my favourites, Ma wears a cream-coloured Mexican dress with a colourful fabric trim she’d bought on a previous trip to Playa del Carmen. Then there was the photo with her blue floppy hat and double-breasted bathing suit. Next to her, my father, holding in his stomach at her request – maybe he wouldn’t look so fat.

That divine Italian tomato sauce could melt in my mouth whenever I was back in town

Now, when I remember my parents, I think of… food. How they had dessert even with breakfast. My father’s love of pizza had him consuming a slice from Gaby’s down the hill every single day.

Maybe that’s another reason why I held on to the apartment, so that divine Italian tomato sauce could melt in my mouth whenever I was back in town. Miraculously, Gaby’s has lasted for decades and it’s a beautiful thing to eat something I’ve loved since I was 10 years old.

Still, I listed the apartment in January 2025. ‘Beautiful grounds, well maintained elevator building, Very Large 1 king size bedroom with two double closets, EIK fits table and chairs, Dining room living room very spacious,’ the ad on Zillow read. Months later, it was sold.

As much as I wanted to savour more than the two big boxes I was shipping back to my tiny guest house in California, I threw away so much… what remained was just a glimmer of who they were.

If only I had a time machine to go back to our days on Francis Lewis Boulevard, in the kitchen where she’d talk to me: ‘Suzie dolly, you are home!’ I grew up trying to adjust to the high anxiety she lived with. It was a good day when we weren’t fighting about, well, everything.

Sometimes, I would do just about anything to get away from her shrill Brooklynese, or beg my father to please share some of the burden – so that maybe he could be bothered by her too, just for a bit. Now, I long to hear her Jewish momma voice. I can hear it exasperating me.

She worried endlessly about me, because she had lost my older brother, her only son

I could taste her temper from a mile away. Her rage was black, like the colour of her permed wavy hair, and when she wasn’t hitting me, I grappled with her fear of what could happen when I walked out the door.

You could die or get stabbed.

‘No Ma.’

You could get mugged on the train.

‘Ma, that’s not goin’ to happen.’

She worried endlessly about me, because she had lost my older brother, her only son, Michael Stuart, who lived for only three weeks before dying in the Brooklyn hospital. I tried to reassure her, bringing flowers and chocolate. But I could not escape.

And yet I missed her scent: a mix of baby powder and Jean Naté. (If you don’t know Jean Naté, go to a drugstore, and look at the bottom shelf, with the cheap imitation perfumes. I’m sure you’ll find a bottle.)

Of course, it was better than the smell of the mothballs she’d put in everything – something her Jewish mothers’ generation was hip to at the time. These were chemical pesticides that a child should never even be near! Did we live in the jungle? Were we being plagued by moths? Every spring, I’d reach into my pockets and find myself still touching a bunch of these balls she’d forgotten to take out.

Argument #20,124: ‘Get rid of the mothballs, Ma.’

Why does it bother you so much?!

‘Because they fucking smell, Ma.’

Don’t use that language with me.

‘Well, you taught it to me.’

In her later years, she realised those mothballs weren’t necessary, but she still didn’t trust me.

Together we would laugh so much… as if we had a secret language no one else shared

‘Ma, let me cook you dinner.’

No, that’s OK, we can eat out.

‘But Ma, I want to.’

You’d probably poison me.

‘Why do you say that, Ma?!’

I was the better cook. Well, at least I knew how to read a recipe. I never did develop a taste for her boiled chicken. She kept all of her mother’s handwritten recipes. I promised to rewrite and save them for her but I never did. I still have every fragment of yellowing pages.

While I tried to talk with her about our oft-antagonistic relationship, she seemed to be mostly unaware of all the times that she’d hit me or called me names. And yet, we were still best friends when she died. I adored teasing her; together we would laugh so much… as if we had a secret language no one else shared.

If she were still alive, I’d want to ask her: ‘Why’d you piss me off so fucking much, Ma?’ I wish we could sit here and eat your favourite tea cookies. I look for you in my dreams. You elicited such intensity, Ma.

It wasn’t that bad, she would say of my childhood.

And sure, that’s true. I did look cute in those black patent-leather shoes, and we did enjoy that slice of blackberry pie to celebrate sixth-grade graduation. I don’t fault you for the bad perm you had me get. Or for throwing out my three-foot-tall Rosie doll after your screaming fit.

It’s just that when you tried to hang me outside the second-storey window to teach me a lesson, you never thought it could trash my soul. There was something wrong with you, Ma. I should have realised that, but I was so small.

What the fuck, Ma. We both should have been better to each other. Why am I alive and you dead? Why did I drive the car that accidentally killed you? After being evacuated twice during the Los Angeles wildfires, what was I holding on to? I could no longer clearly see my Ma standing outside the apartment door, wearing her owl-spectacle glasses, permed black Brillo hair and faded frock, waiting to hug me as I got off the elevator. My parents don’t live in Queens anymore.
